replies.author: IAmFireAndFireIsMe

I don’t get this either. If you have a story but you don’t have the time, resources, money, or and it’s equally the same, the desire to program a game I get it. It’s HARD to create a game. 

But if you have that story. Something you would play. Something that tells a story you want to tell even if it’s a fishing game, a racing game, a horror story that’s fine. Use AI to tell that story but why create something when a better version already exists of something that would rely on thousands of players to make it worth it? 

I don’t get it myself. 

I’ve spent years writing four stories (and a day writing a funny one that I would enjoy) and I’m using AI to help me tell that story in a medium that I think these stories are told best.

However, I can also see the argument that I should shut the hell up and let people do what they want.

Personal preference, let’s just say it’s personal preference.

replies.author: adelie42
replies.body:
Interesting about shuhari!

Similar, long ago I was a Toastmasters district leader and would do both coaching and observations. What confused me for a long time was there seemed to be no correlation between success and following the rules. I eventually discovered it wasn't a function of applying the rules but knowing them. Clubs could do anything they wanted and be successful, but if they didn't know what the best practices were, they tended to be doomed.

replies.author: Recoil42
replies.body: By that you mean people learned to skirt around the rules to the acceptable limits of those rules? Or that the rules didn't matter in the first place?

replies.author: adelie42
replies.body:
No. On one side there was no enforcement. You were expected to self police. The other is that people were paying for an educational program and just not doing it. If you aren't familiar, might not make much sense.

It is a club for corporate professional development with an emphasis on public speaking.

Clubs were encouraged to "make it their own". Every corporate culture is different, and the default was much mlre 1950's cliche business agenda compared to, say, silicon Valley tech bro culture. A lot of it came down to agenda structure. Related, there was a soft expectation to follow Robert's Rules of Order Newly Revised; meetings were supposed to follow parliamentary procedure. Not everyone wanted to do that.

So for example, it is a best practice to print a copy of the agenda for everyone that attends. I saw lots of clubs not do this, but clubs that at least knew they should and didn't tended to have fewer problems. Make any sense?
